sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A struct is a concrete data type with fields and methods. An interface is a set of method requirements; a type satisfies it implicitly by providing those methods.

An interface value carries a dynamic type and a dynamic value. It compares equal to `nil` only when both parts are absent, which explains typed-nil surprises.

For example, a report function that only calls `Write([]byte)` can accept `io.Writer`, allowing a file in production and `bytes.Buffer` in a test without knowing either concrete type.

Interfaces are not required merely to unit-test code, and they should not be created before a real behaviour boundary is known. Prefer interfaces owned near the consuming code.

Accept an interface when the caller needs one small behaviour and multiple implementations are useful, such as a writer, clock, or repository boundary. Keep concrete types when abstraction adds no value.

sections.title: The core model: interfaces and structs in Go
sections.content:
interfaces and structs in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

A struct answers 'what value is this?' while an interface answers 'what can this value do here?' Methods may have value or pointer receivers, which affects which method sets satisfy an interface. No declaration is needed to announce implementation, keeping providers independent from consumers.

Accept an interface when the caller needs one small behaviour and multiple implementations are useful, such as a writer, clock, or repository boundary. Keep concrete types when abstraction adds no value.

For example, a report function that only calls `Write([]byte)` can accept `io.Writer`, allowing a file in production and `bytes.Buffer` in a test without knowing either concrete type.

A concrete parameter exposes one known representation and its full API. An interface parameter accepts any matching behaviour but adds dynamic dispatch and a contract that must be designed deliberately.

sections.title: The practical decision: interfaces and structs in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether interfaces and structs in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

Good interface boundaries appear at variation points: output destination, time source, storage operation, or external client. The consumer should request only what it calls. Returning a concrete value often preserves more capability and lets callers choose which interfaces they need.

A struct is a concrete data type with fields and methods. An interface is a set of method requirements; a type satisfies it implicitly by providing those methods.

Returning a typed nil pointer as an interface produces a non-nil interface value. Very large interfaces also couple callers to methods they do not need and make implementations harder.

For example, a report function that only calls `Write([]byte)` can accept `io.Writer`, allowing a file in production and `bytes.Buffer` in a test without knowing either concrete type.

Return a plain nil interface on no error, check concrete pointers before wrapping them, and reduce interfaces to the methods the caller actually invokes.

Interfaces are not required merely to unit-test code, and they should not be created before a real behaviour boundary is known. Prefer interfaces owned near the consuming code.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: interfaces and structs in Go
sections.content:
Failures around interfaces and structs in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

An interface containing `(*Widget)(nil)` still records the dynamic type `*Widget`, so `value != nil`. A function should avoid returning that typed pointer in the nil case. This issue is visible by printing both dynamic type and value or by testing the error/interface result directly.

sections.title: The important trade-off: interfaces and structs in Go
sections.content:
interfaces and structs in Go and using only concrete types solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Concrete parameters are straightforward and allow compile-time access to the type's complete method set. Interfaces allow substitution and decouple a caller from representation, but a vague abstraction can hide useful operations or encourage runtime assertions. Use the narrowest honest boundary.

sections.title: A reliable diagnosis: interfaces and structs in Go
sections.content:
A good investigation traces the first point where the real state differs from the expected state. With interfaces and structs in Go, that means observing the relevant input, transition, and result rather than guessing from the final symptom.

Start from a caller such as `SendReceipt`. If it only needs `Send(ctx, Message) error`, that single method is the interface. Production and fake senders can both implement it. Lifecycle configuration and unrelated administrative methods remain on concrete types outside the boundary.
